entry.evidence: Herein, we report the assembly of a suite of complementary chromatographic and mass spectrometric methodologies which can be used to intensively examine riverine DOM chemistry

sequences.source_document: Publisher XML full text (jats_text), checked against the published PDF

steps.action: Argue from the literature that targeted and bulk or optical methods leave most DOM uncharacterised, so wider-window untargeted molecular methods are needed.
steps.quote: there is a need for updated molecular-scale methodologies which provide a wider analytical window

steps.action: Assemble a hierarchy of complementary chromatographic and MS methods (GC/MS, GC-FID with GC-Q-TOF, DI-HRMS Orbitrap, py-GC/MS) spanning polarity and molecular weight.
steps.quote: we report the assembly of a suite of complementary chromatographic and mass spectrometric methodologies

steps.action: Choose three contrasting, previously studied UK catchments (peatland, cattle-grazed clay, sewage-impacted clay) as test sites.
steps.quote: three well-researched contrasting UK exemplar field sites were chosen

steps.action: Set four design criteria for the suite and a plastic-free sampling and filtration protocol (pre-combusted glass, GF filters, 0.5 µm pore size).
steps.quote: There were a number of criteria which needed to be fulfilled when designing a robust methodology for untargeted characterisation of riverine DOM.

steps.action: Process HPLC-grade water procedural blanks through every method to check for laboratory contamination.
steps.quote: HPLC grade water was used for procedural blanks which were processed via all the methods described below to check for any laboratory-derived contamination.

steps.action: Build a non-polar protocol: liquid–liquid extraction of filtered water with an internal standard, TMS derivatisation and GC/MS.
steps.quote: The analysis of the non-polar fraction in this programme was carried out using liquid–liquid extraction of ‘raw’ filtered river water.

steps.action: Trial alternative extraction solvents and derivatising reagents; choose n-hexane for immiscibility and MSTFA because BSTFA failed to derivatise urea.
steps.quote: MSTFA was chosen over N,O-bis(trimethylsilyl)trifluoroacetamide (BSTFA)

steps.action: Adapt soil methods for total hydrolysable amino acids and neutral carbohydrates (hydrolysis, derivatisation, GC-FID) to freshwater samples.
steps.quote: Here we refine and test methods previously developed for the determination of amino acids and carbohydrates in soils, adapting them for freshwater samples.

steps.action: Confirm GC-FID compound identities with a second instrument (GC-Q-TOF MS) and with authentic standards.
steps.quote: The samples were also screened using a GC-Quadrupole-Time-of-Flight mass spectrometer (GC-Q-TOF MS)

steps.action: Use the authors' earlier HLB-SPE and positive-mode DI-HRMS Orbitrap protocol and data handling for the polar intermediate-MW fraction.
steps.quote: The analysis of the polar, intermediate molecular weight fraction follows that of Pemberton et al. (80).

steps.action: Apply py-GC/MS, with and without TMAH thermochemolysis, to freeze-dried whole filtered water so that preconcentration is non-selective.
steps.quote: in this study ‘raw’ filtered river water was freeze-dried to dryness

steps.action: Record non-polar total ion chromatograms at the three sites: fatty acid series, sterols and stanols, urea, stearamide, TCIPP.
steps.quote: Figure 3 shows total ion chromatograms gained from the analysis of the non-polar fractions from each of the three contrasting field sites.

steps.action: Match the biomarker distributions to catchment sources using published biomarker meanings: peat plant input, ruminant 5β-stigmastanol, sewage coprostanol, plastic and flame-retardant compounds.
steps.quote: These industrially produced compounds are not observed at either of the other sites further supporting the argument

steps.action: Measure total hydrolysable amino acid concentrations and distributions at Nant y Brwyn and Priors Farm.
steps.quote: A total of 14 hydrolysed amino acids were identified (including the internal standard norleucine) from two of the freeze-dried river water samples

steps.action: Compare amino acid concentrations and compositions with published peatland, DOC and cow-manure profiles.
steps.quote: the relative contributions of each compound at each site agrees with other field sites reported in the literature

steps.action: Repeat amino acid analysis at Chew Stoke; low internal standard recovery shows interference with derivatisation, and the method fails at this site.
steps.quote: despite repeated attempts, at Chew Stoke only a small number of the amino acids were visible from the GC analysis

steps.action: Measure neutral carbohydrate concentrations and distributions at all three sites.
steps.quote: A total of 9 neutral carbohydrates (including myo-inositol as an internal standard) were detected at all three field sites

steps.action: Propose more active microbial communities at impacted sites, with residence time as an alternative, to explain lower building-block concentrations.
steps.quote: where the microbial communities are hypothesised to be particularly active because of the contribution of farm and human wastes

steps.action: Compute deoxysugar/pentose and hexose/pentose ratios and compare them with published plant-versus-microbial thresholds.
steps.quote: confirming the shift from plant-derived carbohydrates at the peatland site towards an increasingly microbially-derived composition

steps.action: After rope contamination of the Nant y Brwyn DI-HRMS sample, substitute another peatland site (Nant Esgair Garn).
steps.quote: As a result, an alternative example is shown here from another well-researched comparative headwater peatland site in mid-Wales

steps.action: Check SPE extraction efficiency by comparing extract DOC with raw-water DOC (58%, 58%, 40.5%).
steps.quote: The extraction efficiency was calculated by measuring the DOC concentration of the extracts following SPE

steps.action: Record DI-HRMS spectra: ion counts, m/z distributions, total ion currents, and the PPG-like 58-unit oligomer series at Chew Stoke.
steps.quote: The ions were extracted from each mass spectrum and yielded a similar number of ions

steps.action: Take the identification of PPG series and pharmaceuticals at Chew Stoke from the authors' earlier HPLC/HRMS/MS study.
steps.quote: These oligomeric series were investigated in more detail by Pemberton et al. (80)

steps.action: Compare shared and unique ion masses across sites (Venn diagram) and read shared ions as ubiquitous DOM and unique ions as source-specific.
steps.quote: It was possible here to compare the number of common masses between the sites to assess the level of similarity

steps.action: Record pyrograms of macromolecular DOM at the three sites and compare relative abundance via the internal standard.
steps.quote: Figure 8 shows pyrograms recorded for each of the three field sites

steps.action: Check the py-GC/MS relative abundance ranking against bulk DOC measurements from prior work (Table 1).
steps.quote: which reflects the DOC measurements at the field sites (See Table 1)

steps.action: Match the pyrolysis products to published peat, pasture-soil and polymer signatures (lignin units, Sphagnum marker, N-containing products, dicarboxylic acids).
steps.quote: This lignin dominated signature is typical of peat landscapes where sedges are present and has been reported previously in the literature

steps.action: List rival origins for the C4–C8 dicarboxylic acids at Chew Stoke (micro/nanoplastic pyrolysis, STW processes, waste-burning aerosol, degraded plastic) without testing them.
steps.quote: It is therefore possible that these compounds have been produced simply as pyrolysis products of micro- or nano-plastics within the waterbody

steps.action: Keep the claim that the suite widens the analytical window and distinguishes DOM source character across contrasting catchments, noting the remaining quantification and coverage gaps.
steps.quote: the data presented here clearly demonstrates the applicability of the methods to distinguish DOM source character and contributions

tree.answer: Molecular composition of riverine DOM, largely uncharacterised beyond a narrow analytical window
Yes, compounds are identified directly by MS and retention times after extraction
Characterise a capability: a complementary method suite tested on contrasting streams
No rivals for the headline claim; untested rival origins only for sub-findings (dicarboxylic acids, low building-block levels)
No distinct predictions derived; source attributions read against known catchment character
Conditions found: three contrasting catchments chosen, one substituted after contamination

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: No repetition by nature; one sample per site per method reported
Limited variation: blanks, GC-Q-TOF confirmation, solvent/reagent trials, extraction efficiency; amino acid method failed at Chew Stoke
Capability kept qualitatively; source attributions are best explanations

end.claim: A complementary suite of GC/MS, GC-FID/GC-Q-TOF, DI-HRMS and py-GC/MS methods widens the analytical window for riverine DOM and distinguishes DOM source character across contrasting catchments, though some DOM remains uncharacterised and the amino acid method fails in sewage-impacted water.

decisive_move.sentence: The assembly and adaptation of the multi-window method suite (steps 2, 6, 8, 11) is what the claim rests on; without it there is no characterised capability to apply to the sites.

gates.evidence: Sites were chosen to demonstrate applicability across contrasting chemistries, not to test a stated hypothesis (§2.1 ¶1). The suite could visibly fail and partly did: amino acids at Chew Stoke (§3.2.1 ¶2) and the rope-contaminated Nant y Brwyn DI-HRMS sample (§3.3 ¶1). But source attributions were checked against catchment character already known, with no benchmark or performance threshold. The design criteria (a)–(d) are stated as set when designing the methods (§2.2 ¶1); nothing else was fixed in advance.

imports.item: Orbitrap Elite hybrid ion trap with heated electrospray, direct-infusion HRMS
GC-Quadrupole-Time-of-Flight accurate-mass MS for confirming identities
Fatty acid amide slip agents (stearamide) migrating from LDPE packaging
Dicarboxylic acids as thermal and photo-oxidation degradation products of polyethylene
Amino acid composition of cow manure (Chen et al. 2003)
C16 and C18 fatty acids as the largest proportion of higher-plant fatty acids

novelty_claims.quote: a wide range of compounds were identified across a range of polarities and molecular weight, thereby extending the analytical window
some of which would not have been identified through targeted analysis
The identification of unexpected compounds, for example the dicarboxylic acids and PPG oligomers at Chew Stoke

limits: No explicit 'first' claims are made; the novelty is framed as an extended analytical window. Sub-claims and their statuses: the source attributions (peat plant input at Nant y Brwyn, ruminant inputs at Priors Farm, sewage effluent at Chew Stoke) are best_explanation, read against catchment character known beforehand. Higher microbial turnover at impacted sites is best_explanation, with residence time as an unexcluded rival, supported only by the co-authors' earlier 14C work. The origin of the dicarboxylic acids is no_conclusion ('currently unknown'). Shared DI-HRMS ions read as ubiquitous natural DOM is an interpretation, not tested. Performance is characterised only qualitatively: apart from SPE extraction efficiency and internal standard behaviour, no detection limits, recoveries, replicate precision or quantification are reported, and quantification is named as the main remaining challenge. Inference: each method appears to have been run on one grab sample per site; sampling dates, replicates and hydrological conditions are not reported. The amino acid method failed at Chew Stoke, and the Nant y Brwyn DI-HRMS sample was replaced by a different site, so the three-site comparison is not matched for DI-HRMS. Internal inconsistencies: (1) py-GC/MS abundance (Nant y Brwyn > Priors Farm > Chew Stoke) is said to reflect DOC, but Table 1 lists Priors Farm DOC (13.7 mg/L) above River Conwy (10.8 mg/L). (2) Priors Farm extraction efficiency is called 'the highest' though it equals Nant Esgair Garn (58%). (3) Distributions are cited as Fig. 4a/4b where Fig. 5a/5b is meant. (4) The C26 alcohol is called 'the dominant fatty acid'. Data are available only on request. No review file was supplied, so the review history is unknown.

disagreements.target: Community expectation that non-polar compounds are absent or negligible in filtered river water
disagreements.support: Non-polar biomarkers (sterols, stanols, fatty acids) are detected in the <0.5 µm fraction at all three sites, which the authors attribute to colloidal material.
disagreements.quote: However, the notion of the purely ‘dissolved’ fraction is flawed

disagreements.target: Operational definition of DOM as material passing a 0.45 µm filter
disagreements.support: The faecal biomarkers found are argued to be colloid-associated rather than truly dissolved, and particulates matter for nutrient cycling (Mena-Rivera et al.).
disagreements.quote: perhaps it is most appropriate to move away from the concept of operationally defined DOM

disagreements.target: Targeted analyses of pesticides, PPCPs and flame retardants in rivers
disagreements.support: Targeted compounds are trace components, leaving most DOM uncharacterised; the untargeted suite found unexpected compounds such as dicarboxylic acids and PPG.
disagreements.quote: These tend to be carried out exclusively on compounds which have been anthropogenically introduced and are of known concern.

disagreements.target: Single-technique protocols, e.g. styrene–divinylbenzene SPE with negative-mode ESI-MS, Py-GC/MS for lignin, SPE-GC/MS (Lynch et al. 2019)
disagreements.support: Each covers a limited window; the paper combines methods to widen it, shown schematically in Fig. 9.
disagreements.quote: Each approach tackles a particular size fraction and class of compounds.

disagreements.target: Common use of cellulose nitrate filters for river water DON/DOP filtration
disagreements.support: Cites the authors' companion paper (Lloyd et al. In press) showing cellulose nitrate filters contaminate molecular-scale analyses, especially py-GC/MS.
disagreements.quote: Cellulose nitrate filters are the most commonly used filter for the filtration of river water samples for DON and DOP analysis.

disagreements.target: SPE isolation of lignin phenols followed by GC/MS or py-GC/MS (Louchouarn et al. 2000; Williams et al. 2016)
disagreements.support: Effective for lignin but selective; freeze-drying whole water gives non-selective recovery of macromolecular DOM.
disagreements.quote: [...] very effective for specifically targeting lignin derived compounds but if a more comprehensive, untargeted approach is desired

disagreements.target: Silvester et al. (2021) peatland river amino acid composition
disagreements.support: Most abundant amino acids agree, but lysine is enriched at Nant y Brwyn, attributed to Sphagnum.
disagreements.quote: The Nant y Brwyn sample did show an increased relative abundance of lysine compared with the literature

disagreements.target: Hedges et al. (1994) and Dittmar et al. (2001) on the dominant amino acids in DOC
disagreements.support: Leucine, valine and proline are additionally elevated at Priors Farm, attributed to cow manure inputs.
disagreements.quote: at Priors Farm the relative abundance of leucine, valine and proline were also increased compared with Nant y Brwyn

alternatives_considered.reason: Cellulose nitrate filters contaminated molecular-scale analyses, most notably py-GC/MS (Lloyd et al. In press)
To match as closely as possible the standard used to define the dissolved fraction
Dichloromethane and n-hexane gave similar chromatograms and the widest range of compounds; n-hexane had better immiscibility

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Drying with a sodium sulphate column
alternatives_considered.reason: A drying step could introduce contaminants and lose compounds by adsorption
BSTFA did not effectively derivatise low molecular weight compounds such as urea; no other differences seen

alternatives_considered.chosen: Total hydrolysable amino acid and carbohydrate pools
alternatives_considered.reason: Free pools assumed extremely small or undetectable in river water (Robarts et al.; Lytle & Perdue)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Freeze-dried whole filtered water for py-GC/MS
alternatives_considered.reason: An untargeted, non-selective preconcentration was desired

alternatives_considered.chosen: Pyrolysis both with and without TMAH thermochemolysis
Oasis HLB SPE with positive-ion DI-HRMS
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Styrene–divinylbenzene SPE with negative-ion ESI (the most common protocol, §1 ¶5)

alternatives_considered.chosen: Nant Esgair Garn peatland sample for DI-HRMS
alternatives_considered.reason: The Nant y Brwyn extract was contaminated during collection, most likely by a rope

alternatives_considered.alternatives: More active or larger microbial pool; longer residence time of inputs
Pyrolysis of micro/nanoplastics; STW treatment processes; plastic-waste burning aerosol; partially oxidised plastic
alternatives_considered.reason: Polymer origin favoured as supported by oligomeric series reported by Pemberton et al. (2020)
